# Health Data Safety Framework (HDSF) rule catalogue.
#
# level:    MUST | SHOULD
# tier:     1 Legal baseline (law in force or adopted) | 2 Forward-compliant (adopted, applying later; guidance;
#           standards) | 3 Best practice
# profiles: core (every product) plus W, M, E, R, T (framework/framework.yaml)
# users:    [all] or some of public, patients, professionals, children
# features: the rule applies only if the product declares one of them in hdsf.yaml
# detection.method: static (code) | manifest (hdsf.yaml) | manual (a person checks) | mixed
#
# HDSF is not legal or regulatory advice. Whether software is a medical device is the manufacturer's decision under
# the MDR or IVDR, and often needs a regulatory expert or a notified body.
version: "0.2.0"
retired: []

rules:
  # ======================================================================= qualification
  - id: CORE-QUA-01
    title: The intended purpose is written down
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product has one written intended purpose: what it is for, for whom, and what it claims to do. The
      same text drives the store listing, the website, the onboarding screens and the qualification decision.
    rationale: >
      Under the MDR and IVDR, whether software is a medical device depends almost entirely on the intended
      purpose the manufacturer claims, not on how the software works (MDCG 2019-11 rev. 1). Without one written
      purpose, nobody can tell which law applies.
    improvement: Write the intended purpose in hdsf.yaml (intended_purpose) and in docs/qualification.md; reuse it word for word in listings.
    effort: low
    sources: [MDR, IVDR, MDCG-2019-11]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: intended_purpose_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-QUA-02
    title: The medical device question is answered and recorded
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Before launch, the maker decides whether the product, or any module of it, is medical device software
      (MDR), in vitro diagnostic software (IVDR), an Annex XVI product, or none of these, and records the
      reasons step by step against the MDCG 2019-11 decision trees. "Undecided" is not a launch state.
    rationale: >
      Placing medical device software on the market without CE marking is illegal; claiming to be a wellness
      app does not help if the intended purpose is medical. MDCG 2019-11 rev. 1 (June 2025) adds modular
      software, disease prevention under Rule 11 and AI.
    improvement: Fill qualification.medical_device and qualification.rationale in hdsf.yaml; use templates/qualification.md. Ask a regulatory expert when in doubt.
    effort: medium
    sources: [MDR, IVDR, MDCG-2019-11]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: qualification_missing, confidence: high}
        - {type: manifest, check: qualification_rationale_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-QUA-03
    title: Claims match the qualification
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Nothing the product or its maker says (store listing, website, adverts, onboarding, AI answers) claims a
      medical purpose the qualification does not cover: diagnosing, treating, monitoring a disease, predicting
      it, or calculating doses.
    rationale: >
      Claims define the intended purpose. A wellness app that markets itself as detecting a disease takes on a
      medical purpose and becomes a medical device without its paperwork. MDCG 2025-4 asks app platforms to keep
      medical device apps apart from wellness apps, based on what the maker declares.
    improvement: Review every public text against the intended purpose before release; keep a list of words the team does not use.
    effort: low
    sources: [MDR, MDCG-2019-11, MDCG-2025-4]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: wellness_purpose_sounds_medical, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-QUA-04
    title: The qualification is checked again when the product changes
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      A new feature, a new claim, a new AI model or a new user group triggers a recorded check of the
      qualification and the class. The check is part of the release checklist.
    rationale: >
      Software changes often, and a small feature (a dose suggestion, a risk score) can change the intended
      purpose. The proposed MDR and IVDR revision also changes software classification rules.
    improvement: Add "qualification still right?" to the release checklist and log the answer in docs/qualification.md.
    effort: low
    sources: [MDCG-2019-11, MDR-REV]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= data protection
  - id: CORE-DAT-01
    title: Health data is identified, including what other data reveals
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The data inventory marks every field that is health, genetic or biometric data, and every field that
      reveals health when linked to a person: orders of medicines or health products, app use itself (using a
      diabetes app), step counts or sleep patterns that show a condition, appointments.
    rationale: >
      Art. 9 GDPR protects data concerning health. The CJEU held that order data for pharmacy-only medicines are
      health data, even without a prescription, when a link to an identifiable person can be made; certainty is
      not needed (C-21/23 Lindenapotheke).
    improvement: Add a health flag to each field in the data inventory; treat "reveals health" fields like health data.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, CJEU-LINDEN]
    gdpr: ['4(15)', '9', '30']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DAT-02
    title: Each use of health data has an Art. 9 condition
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      For each purpose that uses health data, the record names both the Art. 6 legal basis and the Art. 9(2)
      condition (for example explicit consent, health or social care under professional secrecy, public health,
      research). Purposes that have no condition are not carried out.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 9 bans processing of health data unless an Art. 9(2) condition applies. Art. 6 alone is not enough.
    improvement: Fill data.purposes in hdsf.yaml with basis and art9 for each purpose.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['6', '9']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: art9_condition_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-DAT-03
    title: A DPIA is done before launch and kept current
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      A data protection impact assessment covers the product before launch and is updated when features,
      processors or purposes change.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 35. Large-scale processing of health data is high risk by nature; national lists name it.
    improvement: Write docs/dpia.md (templates/dpia-health.md) and link it in hdsf.yaml (data.dpia).
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['35', '36']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: dpia_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-DAT-04
    title: Explicit consent is separate, specific and easy to withdraw
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Where consent is the Art. 9 condition, it is asked separately from the terms, for each purpose, with no
      pre-ticked box, and can be withdrawn in the app as easily as it was given. Refusing optional uses never
      blocks the core service.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 4(11), 7 and 9(2)(a). Explicit consent must be a clear, specific statement.
    improvement: Show one consent screen per optional purpose and a "your choices" page in settings.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['4(11)', '7', '9(2)(a)']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DAT-05
    title: Only the health data the purpose needs is collected
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Each health field has a purpose that needs it. Optional fields are marked optional. Free-text fields are
      avoided where a choice list works. Raw sensor streams are reduced on the device when the purpose only needs
      a summary.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) and 25 (data protection by design and by default).
    improvement: Remove fields without a purpose; make the rest optional where possible; summarise on the device.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['5(1)(c)', '25']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DAT-06
    title: Retention periods are set and enforced
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Every store of health data has a retention period and a job that deletes or anonymises data when it ends,
      including backups and processor copies. National rules for clinical records apply where they exist.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e).
    improvement: Set data.retention in hdsf.yaml and test the deletion job.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['5(1)(e)']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: retention_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-DAT-07
    title: Every processor that receives health data has a contract and is listed
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Each third party (hosting, analytics, support desk, AI provider, crash reporting) is listed with what it
      receives. Those that receive health data have a data processing agreement that covers it.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 28 and 30.
    improvement: List data.third_parties in hdsf.yaml with receives_health_data and a link to the DPA.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['28', '30']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: health_processor_without_dpa, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-DAT-08
    title: Transfers outside the EEA have a legal tool
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Health data is stored in the EEA by default. Any transfer outside it (including support access and AI
      providers) rests on an adequacy decision or another Chapter V tool, documented with a transfer assessment.
    rationale: GDPR Chapter V (Art. 44 to 49).
    improvement: Choose EEA regions; record any non-EEA processor with its transfer tool in hdsf.yaml.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['44', '45', '46', '49']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: transfer_outside_eea, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-DAT-09
    title: People can see, export and delete their data
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      In the product, a person can see their health data, download it in a common machine-readable format and
      delete their account and data. Data from connected devices is part of the export.
    rationale: >
      GDPR Art. 15, 17 and 20. The Data Act gives users of connected products access to the data they generate.
      The EHDS adds rights over electronic health data from 2027.
    improvement: Add export (JSON or FHIR) and delete to account settings; link them in hdsf.yaml (data.rights).
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, DATA-ACT, EHDS]
    gdpr: ['15', '17', '20']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: data_rights_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-DAT-10
    title: No health data in logs, crash reports or debug output
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Logs, crash reports, error trackers and debug output never contain health values, symptoms, diagnoses,
      medications or free text written by the person.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f), 25 and 32. Logs are copied widely and kept longer than the data they describe.
    improvement: Log identifiers and event names only; scrub payloads before they reach the crash reporter.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['5(1)(f)', '32']
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(console\.(log|info|debug|warn)|\bprint|Log\.[dviwe]|logger\.(info|debug|warn)|NSLog|captureMessage)\s*\(.*\b(diagnos\w*|symptom\w*|medication\w*|glucose|blood_?pressure|heart_?rate|pregnan\w*|menstrua\w*|mood_?score|condition)\b'}

  - id: CORE-DAT-11
    title: Analytics and research use pseudonymised data with keys kept apart
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Product analytics and research extracts use random codes instead of identities. The key that links codes
      to people stays in a separate system with separate access. Recipients that cannot re-identify are named
      when the data is collected.
    rationale: >
      Pseudonymised data are still personal data for whoever can re-identify (EDPB Guidelines 01/2025); for a
      recipient without the means, they may not be (CJEU C-413/23 P). The Digital Omnibus proposal would change
      the definition; HDSF does not rely on that change.
    improvement: Generate product-scoped random codes; keep the mapping in a separate store; document who holds what.
    effort: medium
    sources: [EDPB-PSEUDO, CJEU-SRB, GDPR, OMNIBUS-DATA, EDPB-ANON]
    gdpr: ['4(5)', '25', '89']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DAT-12
    title: Health data on the device is encrypted
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Health data stored on a phone, tablet or browser uses encrypted storage (Keychain, Keystore, encrypted
      databases). Plain localStorage, AsyncStorage, SharedPreferences or UserDefaults are not used for it.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 32 (security appropriate to the risk). ISO 27799 applies security controls to health information.
    improvement: Move health values to encrypted storage; keep only non-health settings in plain storage.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, ISO-27799]
    gdpr: ['32']
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, pattern: '(localStorage\.setItem|AsyncStorage\.setItem|getSharedPreferences|UserDefaults\.standard\.set|prefs\.setString)\s*\(\s*[''"][^''"]*(symptom|diagnos|medication|glucose|health|pregnan|cycle|mood|record)'}

  # ======================================================================= tracking and advertising
  - id: CORE-TRK-01
    title: No advertising or tracking SDKs without consent, and none where health data is shown
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Advertising, attribution and cross-app tracking SDKs are not loaded before consent, and never run on
      screens that collect or show health data. Product analytics, if used, is first-party or a processor bound
      by contract, without advertising identifiers.
    rationale: >
      ePrivacy Art. 5(3) covers any access to the device, not only cookies (EDPB Guidelines 2/2023). Studies of
      health apps found most sending data to large platforms, often without saying so (Huckvale 2019; Tangari 2021).
    improvement: Remove ad and attribution SDKs from health products; gate any remaining SDK behind consent and keep it off health screens.
    effort: medium
    sources: [EPRIV, EDPB-ART53, GDPR, R-HUCKVALE2019, R-TANGARI2021]
    gdpr: ['6', '9']
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: dependency, confidence: medium, names: [react-native-fbsdk-next, com.facebook.android:facebook-android-sdk, com.facebook.android:facebook-core, FBSDKCoreKit, FacebookCore, facebook-sdk, '@react-native-firebase/analytics', firebase-analytics, com.google.firebase:firebase-analytics, FirebaseAnalytics, google-mobile-ads, react-native-google-mobile-ads, com.google.android.gms:play-services-ads, Google-Mobile-Ads-SDK, react-native-appsflyer, com.appsflyer:af-android-sdk, AppsFlyerFramework, react-native-adjust, com.adjust.sdk:adjust-android, Adjust, mixpanel, mixpanel-browser, mixpanel-react-native, amplitude-js, '@amplitude/analytics-browser', '@amplitude/analytics-react-native', '@segment/analytics-next', '@segment/analytics-react-native', react-native-branch, io.branch.sdk.android:library, '@hotjar/browser', '@fullstory/browser', logrocket]}
        - {type: manifest, check: trackers_on_health_screens, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-TRK-02
    title: Events sent to analytics do not reveal health
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Event names and properties sent to any analytics or marketing tool do not contain or imply a condition,
      symptom, medication or result ("insulin_logged", "depression_test_done").
    rationale: An event name that names a condition is health data about the person behind the device id (GDPR Art. 9; CJEU C-21/23).
    improvement: Use neutral event names ("entry_saved") and keep health detail in the product's own protected store.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, CJEU-LINDEN]
    gdpr: ['9']
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: high, flags: i, pattern: '(logEvent|trackEvent|\.track|\.capture|setUserProperty)\s*\(\s*[''"][^''"]*(symptom|diagnos|medication|insulin|glucose|pregnan|period|fertil|mood|depress|anxiety|hiv|cancer|therapy)'}

  - id: CORE-TRK-03
    title: No advertising based on health data
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Health data, and data that reveals health, is never used to target, measure or sell advertising, inside or
      outside the product, and is not sold or shared with data brokers.
    rationale: >
      GDPR Art. 9 gives no condition for advertising without explicit consent, and such consent is rarely free. Online
      platforms may not show ads based on profiling with special categories (DSA Art. 26(3)).
    improvement: Remove health-based audiences and segments; state in the privacy notice that health data is never used for ads.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, DSA]
    gdpr: ['9', '21']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: ads_with_health_data, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-TRK-04
    title: Each release is tested for what it actually sends
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Before each release, someone captures the network traffic of a test session and checks that every
      destination and data item is in the privacy notice and the processor list.
    rationale: Only 47% of the user data transmissions of health apps matched their privacy policies in a study of 15,838 apps (Tangari 2021).
    improvement: Add a traffic check (for example with a proxy) to the release checklist; keep the capture with the release.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, R-TANGARI2021, R-HUCKVALE2019]
    gdpr: ['13', '30']
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= security
  - id: CORE-SEC-01
    title: A security policy and a way to report vulnerabilities
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product has a published security contact and vulnerability disclosure policy, and a named person who
      handles reports.
    rationale: >
      GDPR Art. 32. The Cyber Resilience Act requires vulnerability handling for products with digital elements
      (reporting from 11 Sep 2026). NIS2 requires risk management for health entities.
    improvement: Add SECURITY.md and a security.txt on the website; link it in hdsf.yaml (security.policy).
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, CRA, NIS2, IEC-82304-1]
    gdpr: ['32']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: security_policy_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-SEC-02
    title: All traffic is encrypted
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: All network traffic uses TLS. No endpoint uses plain http, except local development.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 32.
    improvement: Replace http:// endpoints with https://; enable HSTS and block cleartext traffic in the app config.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['32']
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, pattern: '[''"]http://(?!localhost|127\.0\.0\.1|10\.|192\.168\.|0\.0\.0\.0|schemas\.|www\.w3\.org|ns\.adobe|purl\.org|xmlns)'}

  - id: CORE-SEC-03
    title: Access to health records needs strong authentication
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Access to stored health data needs a login with protection against guessing. Accounts of health
      professionals and administrators use multi-factor authentication. Sessions on shared devices time out.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 32; NIS2 Art. 21 lists multi-factor authentication among risk management measures. ISO 27799.
    improvement: Enable MFA for staff and professionals; add rate limiting and session timeouts.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, NIS2, ISO-27799]
    gdpr: ['32']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-SEC-04
    title: Breach and incident response is planned and rehearsed
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      A written plan says who decides, who tells the data protection authority within 72 hours, who tells
      affected people, and, where they apply, who reports to the national CSIRT (NIS2) and ENISA (CRA). It is
      rehearsed once a year.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 33 and 34; NIS2 Art. 23 (early warning within 24 hours); CRA Art. 14 (from 11 Sep 2026).
    improvement: Write docs/incident-plan.md and link it in hdsf.yaml (security.incident_plan).
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, NIS2, CRA]
    gdpr: ['33', '34']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: incident_plan_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-SEC-05
    title: Components are listed and security updates are promised
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product keeps a software bill of materials, watches it for known vulnerabilities, and states how long
      it will receive security updates.
    rationale: >
      CRA Annex I (main obligations from 11 Dec 2027; medical devices are outside the CRA but the MDR asks for the
      same). Under the new Product Liability Directive, a missing security update can make software defective.
    improvement: Generate an SBOM in CI (CycloneDX or SPDX); publish the support period.
    effort: medium
    sources: [CRA, PLD, MDR]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: sbom_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-SEC-06
    title: No secrets in the code
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: API keys, private keys and passwords are never committed. They live in a secret store.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 32. A leaked key often opens the whole health database.
    improvement: Move secrets to the platform's secret store; rotate any key that was ever committed.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['32']
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: high, pattern: '(sk-(proj-|ant-)?[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{20,}|AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|AIza[0-9A-Za-z_\-]{35}|-----BEGIN (RSA |EC )?PRIVATE KEY-----)'}

  - id: CORE-SEC-07
    title: Access to health records is logged
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Every read and change of a person's health record by staff or professionals is logged with who, when and
      why, and the logs are reviewed.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 5(2) and 32 (accountability and security). The EHDS makes such logging mandatory for EHR systems (see E-LOG-01).
    improvement: Add an audit log for record access; review it monthly; keep it tamper-evident.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, EHDS, ISO-27799]
    gdpr: ['5(2)', '32']
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= AI
  - id: CORE-AI-01
    title: Every AI component is listed
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative, ai_clinical]
    requirement: >
      An AI inventory lists each model, its provider, purpose, inputs (health data or not), outputs, human
      oversight and AI Act role. Provider settings for retention and training are recorded.
    rationale: >
      AI Act Art. 4 (AI literacy measures) and the provider and deployer duties that follow from the role. GDPR
      Art. 5 and 35 when health data goes into a model.
    improvement: Create docs/ai-inventory.md and link it in hdsf.yaml (ai.inventory).
    effort: low
    sources: [AIA, GDPR]
    gdpr: ['30', '35']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: ai_without_inventory, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-AI-02
    title: AI says it is AI, and not a clinician, from the first message
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      A chatbot, agent or AI character tells people from the first interaction that it is AI and not a doctor,
      nurse or therapist, in plain words, and repeats it when the topic turns to symptoms or treatment. Generated
      images and audio carry machine-readable marks.
    rationale: >
      AI Act Art. 50, applicable from 2 Aug 2026; the Commission's guidelines read the "obvious" exception
      narrowly. People who are ill or worried are more likely to over-trust an answer.
    improvement: Add a persistent AI label and a first-message notice; mark generated media.
    effort: low
    sources: [AIA, AIA-GL-ART50]
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: dependency, confidence: medium, names: [openai, '@anthropic-ai/sdk', anthropic, '@google/generative-ai', '@google/genai', google-generativeai, '@mistralai/mistralai', mistralai, groq-sdk, ai, '@ai-sdk/openai', langchain, '@langchain/core']}

  - id: CORE-AI-03
    title: A general chatbot does not diagnose or advise treatment
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      Unless the product is qualified as a medical device for that purpose, its AI does not give a diagnosis, a
      risk score for a disease, a dose or a treatment change for an individual. It gives general information and
      points to a professional. The limits are tested with red-team prompts before each model change.
    rationale: >
      Personalised diagnosis or treatment advice is a medical intended purpose (MDR Art. 2(1); MDCG 2019-11). The
      MDCG and the AI Board confirm that AI with a medical purpose must meet both the MDR and the AI Act (MDCG 2025-6).
    improvement: Add system instructions and output checks for diagnosis and dosing; keep a test set of risky prompts and run it in CI.
    effort: medium
    sources: [MDR, MDCG-2019-11, MDCG-2025-6]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-AI-04
    title: AI providers do not keep or train on health data
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative, ai_clinical]
    requirement: >
      Health data sent to an AI provider is covered by a processing agreement, zero or minimal retention, and no
      training on it. Health data of users is not used to train or fine-tune the maker's own models without a DPIA,
      an Art. 9 condition and, for research, approval.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 5, 9, 28 and 35.
    improvement: Choose enterprise or zero-retention settings; record them in the AI inventory.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['9', '28']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-AI-05
    title: AI does not exploit illness, age or distress
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative, ai_clinical]
    requirement: >
      AI features do not use manipulative techniques, or exploit vulnerability due to age, disability, illness or a
      difficult situation, to change what people do in a way that harms them (for example pushing purchases or
      stopping treatment).
    rationale: AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) and (b), applicable since 2 Feb 2025; Commission guidelines on prohibited practices.
    improvement: Review prompts, reward signals and upsell logic of AI features; document the review.
    effort: low
    sources: [AIA, AIA-GL-PROHIB]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= safety and content
  - id: CORE-SAF-01
    title: People can always find urgent help
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [symptom_input, mental_health, ai_generative, emergency_content, chat]
    requirement: >
      Where people enter symptoms, talk about mental health or chat (with AI or people), the product shows how to
      get urgent help (112 and national lines) in one tap, and says the product is not an emergency service.
      Words that signal danger lead to that help, not to a generic answer.
    rationale: >
      A product that fails to point to urgent help when someone describes an emergency can be found defective
      under the new Product Liability Directive (psychological harm counts). ISO/TS 82304-2 assesses health
      safety in apps.
    improvement: Add a help button and an emergency route; list it in hdsf.yaml (safety.emergency_route); test it in each language.
    effort: low
    sources: [PLD, ISO-82304-2]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: emergency_route_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-SAF-02
    title: Health content is reviewed by a qualified person and dated
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Health information in the product is written or reviewed by a named, qualified professional, cites its
      sources and shows when it was last reviewed. Reviews happen at least yearly.
    rationale: ISO/TS 82304-2 asks for evidence of content quality; the Label2Enable scheme assesses it.
    improvement: Record reviewer, date and sources per content page; link the register in hdsf.yaml (safety.content_review).
    effort: medium
    sources: [ISO-82304-2, LABEL2ENABLE]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: content_review_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-SAF-03
    title: Evidence of benefit fits the claims
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Each benefit the product claims is backed by evidence of a fitting strength (user studies, trials,
      real-world data), published or available to professionals who recommend it.
    rationale: ISO/TS 82304-2 and health app assessment schemes ask for evidence of benefit; MDCG 2020-1 sets the bar for medical device software.
    improvement: Keep an evidence register per claim; prefer outcomes over engagement.
    effort: high
    sources: [ISO-82304-2, MDCG-2020-1, LABEL2ENABLE]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= communication and design
  - id: CORE-COM-01
    title: People are told in plain words what happens to their health data
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Before the first health data is collected, a short plain-language notice says what is collected, why, who
      receives it, where it is stored and for how long. The full privacy notice is one tap away.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 12 and 13. 28% of free health apps studied had no privacy policy at all (Tangari 2021).
    improvement: Add a one-screen summary before onboarding asks for health data; test it with users.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, R-TANGARI2021]
    gdpr: ['12', '13', '14']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-COM-02
    title: No dark patterns around consent, cancellation or worry
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Consent, subscription and cancellation flows are neutral: equal buttons, no confirm-shaming, no fear-based
      messages about health to drive purchases, cancellation as easy as sign-up.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 7 (freely given consent); DSA Art. 25 bans dark patterns on online platforms.
    improvement: Review flows against a dark pattern checklist; make refusing and cancelling one step.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, DSA]
    gdpr: ['7']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-COM-03
    title: Notifications do not reveal health on the lock screen
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [notifications, medication]
    requirement: >
      By default, notifications say nothing about a condition, medication or result ("Time for your check-in", not
      "Take your HIV medication"). People can choose more detail.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) and 25. A lock screen is often seen by others.
    improvement: Use neutral default texts; offer a detailed mode in settings.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['5(1)(f)', '25']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-ACC-01
    title: The product is accessible
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product meets WCAG 2.2 level AA (EN 301 549). Public sector bodies publish an accessibility statement.
      Health information is also offered in plain language.
    rationale: >
      People with disabilities and long-term conditions use health products more than most. Public hospitals and
      health services must meet EN 301 549 (Directive (EU) 2016/2102); some services fall under the European
      Accessibility Act.
    improvement: Test with screen readers and large text; fix contrast and target sizes; publish a statement.
    effort: medium
    sources: [WAD, EAA, EN301549, WCAG22]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= governance
  - id: CORE-GOV-01
    title: Named people are responsible for data protection and safety
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product names who is responsible for data protection, security and (for devices) regulatory
      compliance. A data protection officer is appointed where health data is processed at large scale as a core
      activity.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 37(1)(c); MDR Art. 15 (person responsible for regulatory compliance) for devices.
    improvement: Record the names in hdsf.yaml (governance) and in the privacy notice.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, MDR]
    gdpr: ['37', '38', '39']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-GOV-02
    title: The manifest and the qualification are reviewed every year
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: hdsf.yaml, the qualification and the DPIA are reviewed at least once a year and after any major change.
    rationale: Law and guidance in digital health move fast (EHDS from 2027, AI Act high-risk dates, MDR revision).
    improvement: Set review.last_reviewed in hdsf.yaml and a calendar reminder.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, EHDS, MDR-REV]
    gdpr: ['24', '35']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: review_stale, confidence: medium}

  # ======================================================================= children
  - id: CORE-CHD-01
    title: Products used by children also meet the CSEF core
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [children]
    requirement: >
      When children use the product, it also meets the core rules of the Child-Safe EdTech Framework that fit it
      (age assurance, parental consent below the national age, design and communication rules), and records
      the CSEF check.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 8 and recital 38 give children specific protection. CSEF turns the EU rules for children's digital products into checkable rules.
    improvement: Run the CSEF scan or the CSEF Workbench; link the report in hdsf.yaml (children.csef_report).
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, CSEF]
    gdpr: ['8']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: children_without_csef, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-CHD-02
    title: Teenagers' confidential health topics stay confidential
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [children]
    requirement: >
      Parent or guardian access to a teenager's data follows national law on consent and confidentiality for
      health care. Topics such as sexual health, mental health and substance use are not shown to parents by
      default where the teenager may consult on their own.
    rationale: >
      Children have data protection rights of their own (GDPR recital 38). National rules on when minors can
      consent to care differ; the product follows the country where it is used.
    improvement: Map national ages and rules per country; give teenagers a private space for confidential topics.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, CSEF]
    gdpr: ['8', '12']
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= W: wellness and lifestyle
  - id: W-QUA-01
    title: A wellness product stays wellness
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [W]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product does not add features that serve a medical purpose for an individual (diagnosis, disease
      monitoring, dose calculation, treatment decisions) without a new qualification. General fitness, sleep,
      diet and wellbeing features are fine.
    rationale: MDCG 2019-11 rev. 1 explains when software for lifestyle or wellbeing remains outside the MDR, and when disease prevention brings it under Rule 11.
    improvement: Keep a list of feature ideas that would need re-qualification; route them through CORE-QUA-04.
    effort: low
    sources: [MDR, MDCG-2019-11]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: W-QUA-02
    title: Wellness texts make no medical claims
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [W]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Store texts, screens and notifications of a wellness product do not say it diagnoses, detects, treats or
      cures a disease, or that it is "medical grade" or "clinically proven", unless that is true and qualified.
    rationale: Claims make the intended purpose (MDR; MDCG 2019-11). MDCG 2025-4 asks platforms to list wellness apps apart from medical device apps.
    improvement: Search the texts for medical claims before each release and rewrite them.
    effort: low
    sources: [MDR, MDCG-2019-11, MDCG-2025-4]
    detection:
      method: static
      patterns:
        - {type: regex, confidence: medium, flags: i, globs: ['*.json', '*.strings', '*.xml', '*.arb', '*.po', '*.html', '*.yaml', '*.yml', '*.properties'], pattern: '\b(diagnos(e|es|is|ing)\b|detects? (cancer|diabetes|arrhythmia|atrial fibrillation|depression|sleep apnea)|cures? |treats? (depression|anxiety|diabetes|insomnia)|clinically proven|medical[- ]grade)'}

  - id: W-EHD-01
    title: Interoperability with health records is claimed only with the EHDS label
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [W]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      If the product claims it works with electronic health record systems, it meets the EHDS essential
      requirements and common specifications, carries the EHDS label, informs users of what the
      interoperability means, and is registered in the EU database.
    rationale: EHDS Art. 47 to 49 (labelling of wellness applications); applies in stages from 26 Mar 2027.
    improvement: Either drop the claim or plan the EHDS conformity work and label; record it in hdsf.yaml (ehds).
    effort: high
    sources: [EHDS]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: wellness_interop_without_label, confidence: high}

  - id: W-EHD-02
    title: Data goes to a health record only when the person chooses
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [W]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Being interoperable never means automatic sharing. Each transfer of wellness data to an EHR system, or to a
      professional, happens only after the person chooses it, and they can choose which data.
    rationale: EHDS Art. 48(2). The EDPB and EDPS asked for strong limits on the use of wellness data (Joint Opinion 03/2022).
    improvement: Add a share screen with data choices; log each share; allow stopping future shares.
    effort: medium
    sources: [EHDS, EDPB-EDPS-EHDS]
    gdpr: ['7']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: W-DAT-01
    title: Data from wearables and sensors is accessible to the user
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [W]
    users: [all]
    features: [wearables, sensors]
    requirement: >
      Users can get the data their connected device or related service generates, easily, securely and free,
      and can have it shared with a third party they choose. Products placed on the market from 12 Sep 2026 make
      this possible by design.
    rationale: Data Act Art. 3 to 5, applicable from 12 Sep 2025 (design duty from 12 Sep 2026).
    improvement: Offer a data download and a documented sharing route; tell users before purchase what data the product generates.
    effort: medium
    sources: [DATA-ACT]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: W-SEC-01
    title: Connected wellness products meet the Cyber Resilience Act
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [W]
    users: [all]
    features: [wearables, sensors]
    requirement: >
      Connected wellness devices and their apps meet the CRA essential requirements by 11 Dec 2027: secure by
      default, security updates, vulnerability handling, and reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities from
      11 Sep 2026.
    rationale: CRA; medical devices are outside it, wellness products with digital elements generally are not.
    improvement: Run a CRA gap analysis; decide the conformity route and support period.
    effort: high
    sources: [CRA]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: W-DAT-02
    title: Reproductive, sexual and mental health data stays on the device by default
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [W]
    users: [all]
    features: [reproductive_health, mental_health, genetic]
    requirement: >
      Cycle, fertility, pregnancy, sexual health, mental health and genetic data is stored on the device by
      default. Cloud sync and backup are opt-in, end-to-end encrypted where possible, and explained.
    rationale: >
      These are the most sensitive health data and the most often misused (GDPR Art. 9). Apps for depression were
      found sending data to large platforms without saying so (Huckvale 2019).
    improvement: Make local storage the default; add an explained opt-in for sync with end-to-end encryption.
    effort: high
    sources: [GDPR, R-HUCKVALE2019]
    gdpr: ['9', '25', '32']
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= M: medical device software
  - id: M-QUA-01
    title: The class is assigned with reasons
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The software has a class under MDR Annex VIII (Rule 11 for most software) or IVDR Annex VIII, with the
      reasons written down, and the conformity route that follows from it.
    rationale: MDR Art. 51 and Annex VIII; MDCG 2019-11 rev. 1. Most software above class I needs a notified body.
    improvement: Fill qualification.class in hdsf.yaml and keep the reasoning in docs/qualification.md.
    effort: medium
    sources: [MDR, IVDR, MDCG-2019-11]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: device_class_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: M-QMS-01
    title: A quality management system covers the software life cycle
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The manufacturer runs a quality management system (ISO 13485) with a software life cycle process (IEC
      62304): requirements, architecture, verification, release, maintenance and problem resolution.
    rationale: MDR Art. 10(9) and Annex IX; harmonised standards give presumption of conformity.
    improvement: Set up the QMS before development of the device version; map the existing process to IEC 62304.
    effort: high
    sources: [MDR, ISO-13485, IEC-62304]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: device_docs_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: M-RSK-01
    title: Risk management covers clinical, use and security risks
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      A risk management file (ISO 14971) covers wrong outputs, use errors, misuse, cybersecurity and data
      quality, with controls and residual risk accepted by a named person.
    rationale: MDR Annex I, Chapter I and section 17 (software and cybersecurity).
    improvement: Keep docs/risk-management.md under change control; review it with each release.
    effort: high
    sources: [MDR, ISO-14971]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: M-CLN-01
    title: Clinical evaluation follows MDCG 2020-1
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      A clinical (or performance) evaluation shows valid clinical association, technical performance and clinical
      performance for the intended purpose, and is updated with post-market data.
    rationale: MDR Art. 61 and Annex XIV; IVDR Art. 56; MDCG 2020-1 for software.
    improvement: Write the clinical evaluation plan and report; link them in hdsf.yaml (clinical).
    effort: high
    sources: [MDR, IVDR, MDCG-2020-1]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: clinical_evaluation_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: M-PMS-01
    title: Post-market surveillance and vigilance are running
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      A post-market surveillance plan collects complaints, incidents, app reviews and performance data; serious
      incidents are reported to the competent authority on time; trends are analysed.
    rationale: MDR Art. 83 to 92.
    improvement: Route support tickets and store reviews into the PMS process; name who reports incidents.
    effort: medium
    sources: [MDR]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: M-APP-01
    title: The store listing shows device information before download
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      In app stores and on the website, before download, people see the device name, manufacturer, intended
      purpose, CE marking, warnings and the electronic instructions for use. The app is listed as a medical
      device, apart from wellness apps.
    rationale: Uploading a device app to a platform is placing it on the market (MDCG 2025-4); MDR Art. 7 and Annex I section 23.
    improvement: Update store listings and the in-app "about" screen with the device information.
    effort: low
    sources: [MDR, MDCG-2025-4]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: M-AI-01
    title: Medical AI is ready for the AI Act high-risk rules
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_clinical]
    requirement: >
      Medical device AI that needs a notified body meets the AI Act high-risk requirements (risk management,
      data governance, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy and robustness) by 2 Aug 2028, inside one
      technical file with the MDR documentation.
    rationale: >
      Such AI is high-risk under AI Act Art. 6(1); the AI Act does not change the MDR class (MDCG 2025-6). The AI
      Omnibus sets 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I products.
    improvement: Add the AI Act sections to the technical file now; link the AI risk file in hdsf.yaml (ai.risk_file).
    effort: high
    sources: [AIA, AIA-OMNIBUS, MDCG-2025-6]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: medical_ai_without_risk_file, confidence: high}

  - id: M-AI-02
    title: Changes to models are controlled
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_clinical]
    requirement: >
      Retraining, new models and new data sources go through change control with an assessment of whether the
      change is significant, and with verification on a locked test set before release.
    rationale: MDR Annex IX (changes to approved devices need notified body review when they are substantial); MDCG 2025-6 on AI changes.
    improvement: Version models and datasets; write the change assessment template; never auto-deploy a retrained model.
    effort: medium
    sources: [MDR, MDCG-2025-6]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: M-WCH-01
    title: The MDR and IVDR revision is tracked
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: Someone follows the targeted MDR and IVDR revision and reports changes to classification and software rules to the team.
    rationale: The Commission proposal of 16 Dec 2025 changes software classification and other rules; it is with Parliament and Council.
    improvement: Add the procedure to a watch list; review at each quarterly planning.
    effort: low
    sources: [MDR-REV]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= E: EHR systems and EHDS
  - id: E-INT-01
    title: The EHR system meets the EHDS essential requirements
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [E]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      An EHR system has the European interoperability component and the European logging component (EHDS Annex
      II), passes the digital testing environment, and carries the EU declaration of conformity and CE marking
      before it is placed on the market under the EHDS dates.
    rationale: EHDS Chapter III; the Commission describes European digital testing environments for manufacturers.
    improvement: Plan the conformity work against the EHDS dates; link the evidence in hdsf.yaml (ehds.conformity).
    effort: high
    sources: [EHDS]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: ehr_without_ehds_conformity, confidence: high}

  - id: E-INT-02
    title: Data leaves in the European exchange format, without lock-in
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [E]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The system exports priority categories (patient summaries, ePrescriptions, images, lab results, discharge
      reports) in the European electronic health record exchange format, and customers can switch provider
      without losing data or paying exit fees.
    rationale: EHDS (exchange format); Data Act Chapter VI (switching between data processing services).
    improvement: Implement the exchange format (FHIR based where specified); document the exit plan for customers.
    effort: high
    sources: [EHDS, DATA-ACT, HL7-FHIR]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: E-LOG-01
    title: People can see who accessed their record
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [E]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Every access to a person's electronic health data is logged, and the person can see who accessed it and
      when.
    rationale: EHDS (logging component and the right to information on access); GDPR Art. 15.
    improvement: Expose the access log in the patient portal; alert on unusual access.
    effort: medium
    sources: [EHDS, GDPR]
    gdpr: ['15']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: E-ACC-01
    title: People can restrict who sees parts of their record
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [E]
    users: [all]
    requirement: The system lets people restrict access by professionals to all or part of their data, with an emergency override that is logged.
    rationale: EHDS rights of natural persons over their electronic health data (primary use).
    improvement: Add per-category restrictions and a logged break-glass route.
    effort: high
    sources: [EHDS]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: E-DAT-01
    title: Professionals see records only in a care relationship
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [E, T]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Professionals can open a person's record only when they are part of that person's care, under professional
      secrecy, and only the parts they need.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 9(2)(h) and 9(3).
    notes:
      - "Portugal: only health professionals may access the clinical record (Lei 12/2005, Art. 5); access on a need-to-know basis (Lei 58/2019, Art. 29)."
    improvement: Tie access rights to care episodes; review access rights monthly.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, PT-LEI-12-2005, PT-LEI-58-2019]
    gdpr: ['9(2)(h)', '9(3)']
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= R: research and secondary use
  - id: R-DAT-01
    title: Research uses have a legal basis and approval
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [R, core]
    users: [all]
    features: [research_use]
    requirement: >
      Each research use of health data has an Art. 6 basis, an Art. 9(2) condition (often (j) with national
      safeguards, or explicit consent), ethics approval where required, and a protocol. Research use is not
      hidden inside the terms of service.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 9(2)(j) and 89. The EDPB's draft research guidelines (1/2026) are under consultation.
    improvement: Record each study in hdsf.yaml (research) with basis, approval and protocol.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, EDPB-RESEARCH]
    gdpr: ['9(2)(j)', '89']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: research_without_approval, confidence: high}

  - id: R-DAT-02
    title: Care data and research data are kept apart
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [R]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Researchers receive pseudonymised extracts with only the fields the protocol needs, in a separate
      environment. The re-identification key stays with the care system.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 25 and 89(1); EDPB Guidelines 01/2025 on pseudonymisation; CJEU C-413/23 P.
    improvement: Build an extract pipeline with field selection and codes; restrict research environments.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, EDPB-PSEUDO, CJEU-SRB]
    gdpr: ['25', '89']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: R-DAT-03
    title: Only group results are published
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [R]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Published results and open datasets hold group figures only, with small groups suppressed or merged, and are
      checked for re-identification before release.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 89; EHDS secondary use allows only anonymised or pseudonymised data in secure processing environments.
    improvement: Set minimum group sizes; add a disclosure check to the publication step.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, EHDS, EDPB-ANON]
    gdpr: ['89']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: R-EHD-01
    title: The maker is ready to be an EHDS data holder
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [R, E, W]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The maker knows whether it will be a health data holder under the EHDS, can describe its datasets, and has
      a plan for answering health data access bodies, including for wellness data.
    rationale: EHDS secondary use rules (from 2029 and 2031) cover data from wellness applications too; the EDPB and EDPS asked for limits on that.
    improvement: Write a short dataset description and a contact process for data access bodies.
    effort: medium
    sources: [EHDS, EDPB-EDPS-EHDS]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: R-CLN-01
    title: Clinical investigations of devices follow the MDR
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [R, M]
    users: [patients, public]
    requirement: >
      A study to gather clinical evidence for medical device software follows MDR Chapter VI: protocol, ethics
      committee opinion, competent authority notification or authorisation, informed consent, and safety reporting.
    rationale: MDR Art. 62 to 82.
    improvement: Plan the investigation with the competent authority's procedure (INFARMED in Portugal).
    effort: high
    sources: [MDR]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= T: telehealth and care delivery
  - id: T-DAT-01
    title: Remote consultations are private
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [T]
    users: [all]
    features: [telehealth]
    requirement: >
      Video, audio and chat consultations are encrypted in transit, ideally end to end, are not recorded without
      the patient's informed agreement, and do not run through consumer tools without a processing agreement.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 9(2)(h), 28 and 32; ISO 27799.
    improvement: Use a health-grade video provider under a DPA; turn recording off by default.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, ISO-27799]
    gdpr: ['9(2)(h)', '28', '32']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: T-DAT-02
    title: Remote care is recorded in the clinical record
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [T]
    users: [patients]
    features: [telehealth]
    requirement: The outcome of each remote consultation is recorded in the clinical record as national law requires, and the patient can access it.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 15. National law on clinical records applies.
    notes:
      - "Portugal: health information, including clinical data, belongs to the person (Lei 12/2005, Art. 3)."
    improvement: Integrate the consultation notes with the record system; give patients access.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR, PT-LEI-12-2005]
    gdpr: ['15']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: T-SEC-01
    title: Care providers meet NIS2
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [T]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      A care provider in scope of NIS2 (and its national law) registers with the national authority, applies the
      risk management measures, reports significant incidents and trains its management body.
    rationale: NIS2 Art. 20, 21 and 23; health is a sector of high criticality.
    notes:
      - "Portugal: Decreto-Lei n.º 125/2025, in force 3 Apr 2026, with CNCS Regulamento n.º 756/2026; management bodies can be personally liable."
    improvement: Check scope and register; map measures to the national reference framework.
    effort: high
    sources: [NIS2, PT-NIS2]
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: nis2_status_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: T-GOV-01
    title: Professionals on the platform are verified
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [T]
    users: [all]
    requirement: The platform checks the identity and licence of each professional before they see patients, and re-checks yearly.
    rationale: Health app assessment frameworks look at who gives care and with what qualification (ISO/TS 82304-2).
    improvement: Check against the national register (Ordem dos Médicos and others in Portugal); show the licence in the profile.
    effort: medium
    sources: [ISO-82304-2]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= GDPR (RGPD) gaps, v0.2
  - id: CORE-DAT-13
    title: Processing of health data is recorded
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The maker keeps a record of processing activities: purposes, categories of people and data (health data
      marked), recipients, transfers, retention and security measures. It is kept current.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 30. The exemption for small organisations does not apply to processing of special categories such as health data.
    improvement: Keep the record (a table is enough) and link it in hdsf.yaml (data.records).
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['30']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: records_missing, confidence: high}

  - id: CORE-DAT-14
    title: No automated decision with serious effects without safeguards
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_clinical, ai_generative]
    requirement: >
      The product does not take decisions based only on automated processing of health data that have legal or
      similarly significant effects on a person (access to care, priority, cover, eligibility), unless the person
      gave explicit consent or the law allows it, and then with human review on request, a way to contest, and
      clear information about the logic involved.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 22, including Art. 22(4) on special categories; Art. 13(2)(f) on information about the logic.
    improvement: Map every automated decision; add human review and a contest route; explain the logic in plain words.
    effort: medium
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['13(2)(f)', '22']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DAT-15
    title: Data protection roles are clear
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      For each use of health data, the maker knows whether it acts as controller, processor or joint controller
      (for example with a clinic or an insurer), and the contracts say so. A maker outside the EU names an EU
      representative.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 24, 26, 27 and 28. In digital health, the same app can be the clinic's processor for care and its own controller for analytics.
    improvement: Write a roles table per purpose; set data.gdpr_role in hdsf.yaml; sign joint controller arrangements where needed.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR]
    gdpr: ['24', '26', '27', '28']
    detection:
      method: manifest
      patterns:
        - {type: manifest, check: roles_missing, confidence: medium}

  - id: CORE-DAT-16
    title: Requests from people are answered within a month
    level: MUST
    tier: 1
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      People can ask to correct, restrict, object to or get a copy of their data through a simple route, and get an
      answer within one month. The product tells them they can complain to the data protection authority.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 12(3), 16, 18, 21 and 77.
    notes:
      - "Portugal: the supervisory authority is the CNPD (Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados)."
    improvement: Add a privacy request form or address; track requests and answer times.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, PT-LEI-58-2019]
    gdpr: ['12', '16', '18', '21', '77']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DAT-17
    title: Data protection is part of design decisions
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Design reviews ask what data each feature needs, choose the most protective default, and record the choice.
      Privacy-friendly settings are on by default; more sharing is opt-in.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 25 and the EDPB guidelines on data protection by design and by default.
    improvement: Add a data question to the design review template; list the defaults and why.
    effort: low
    sources: [GDPR, EDPB-DPBD]
    gdpr: ['25']
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= Layer 2: EU recommendations and guidance
  - id: CORE-AI-06
    title: AI built with personal data passes the EDPB tests
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative, ai_clinical]
    requirement: >
      When the maker trains, fine-tunes or evaluates an AI model with personal data, it documents the legal basis
      (for legitimate interest: the three-step test), checks whether the model can be considered anonymous before
      claiming so, and checks that any third-party model it uses was not built unlawfully.
    rationale: >
      EDPB Opinion 28/2024 sets the approach supervisory authorities use for AI models. The bar for an anonymous
      model is high. Health data adds the Art. 9 condition, which the opinion does not cover.
    improvement: "Keep an AI data sheet per model: data sources, legal basis, Art. 9 condition, anonymity assessment, supplier checks."
    effort: medium
    sources: [EDPB-AIMODELS, GDPR]
    gdpr: ['5', '6', '9', '35']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-AI-07
    title: No scraped health data without an Art. 9 condition
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative, ai_clinical, research_use]
    requirement: >
      The product and its maker do not scrape or extract health data from websites, forums, social media or other
      apps for AI, analytics or research without an Art. 9(2) condition. Any scraping is limited to reliable,
      named sources, keeps timestamps, validates the data and is explained to the people concerned.
    rationale: >
      The EDPB's draft guidelines on web scraping for generative AI (03/2026) require both an Art. 6 basis and an
      Art. 9(2) exception when scraping touches special categories, with attention to purpose limitation and
      transparency.
    improvement: List every external data source; remove scrapers that may collect health data; document the conditions for the rest.
    effort: medium
    sources: [EDPB-SCRAPE, EDPB-AIMODELS, GDPR]
    gdpr: ['5(1)(b)', '6', '9', '14']
    detection:
      method: mixed
      patterns:
        - {type: dependency, confidence: medium, names: [scrapy, beautifulsoup4, bs4, cheerio, crawlee, apify-client, newspaper3k, trafilatura, snscrape]}

  - id: CORE-AI-08
    title: Health AI is tested with its intended users
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    features: [ai_generative, ai_clinical]
    requirement: >
      Before release and after each model change, AI features are tested with the people who will use them, for
      accuracy, bias across groups, and understanding of the limits. The limits are written in the product.
    rationale: The WHO guidance on large multi-modal models asks developers to design and test for all intended users and to be transparent about limits.
    improvement: Build a test set from real (consented) use cases; report results by group; publish a short limits statement.
    effort: medium
    sources: [WHO-LMM, AIA]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-LNG-01
    title: Health information is in plain language
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Health information, instructions and notices use short sentences, common words, the active voice and
      explained terms. Medical terms are explained the first time.
    rationale: >
      Almost half of people in an eight-country EU survey had limited health literacy (HLS-EU). The Commission's
      clear writing guide and the Publications Office plain language guide set the EU approach. GDPR Art. 12
      already requires clear and plain language for privacy information.
    improvement: Run the Workbench language check on your texts; rewrite long sentences; keep a glossary.
    effort: low
    sources: [EC-CLEAR, OP-PLAIN, R-HLS-EU2015, GDPR]
    gdpr: ['12']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-LNG-02
    title: The product speaks its users' languages
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product is offered in the languages of the countries where it is used. Health content and safety messages
      are translated or reviewed by a qualified person, not only by machine translation.
    rationale: Information people cannot read is not information. ISO/TS 82304-2 assesses whether health information is understandable for the intended users.
    improvement: List countries and languages in hdsf.yaml; record who reviewed each translation of health content.
    effort: medium
    sources: [OP-PLAIN, ISO-82304-2]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-SAF-04
    title: Health recommendations follow recognised guidance
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Advice the product gives (exercise, diet, sleep, medication reminders, mental health tips) follows recognised
      guidance from public health bodies or clinical guidelines, and shows its source and date to the user.
    rationale: ISO/TS 82304-2 assesses the quality and sources of health information; the WHO guidance asks for transparency about where AI health answers come from.
    improvement: Link each recommendation to its guideline in the content register; show "Source and date" in the product.
    effort: medium
    sources: [ISO-82304-2, WHO-LMM]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-COM-04
    title: Consent and privacy screens avoid deceptive design
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Consent, privacy settings and sign-up screens avoid the deceptive patterns the EDPB names: too many requests,
      hidden options, emotional steering, obstructed choices, inconsistent wording, and missing information.
    rationale: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a), 7, 12 and 25 as read by the EDPB in Guidelines 03/2022 and 05/2020.
    improvement: Review each screen against the EDPB categories; fix the worst first; keep screenshots as evidence.
    effort: medium
    sources: [EDPB-DECEPTIVE, EDPB-CONSENT, GDPR, DSA]
    gdpr: ['5(1)(a)', '7', '12', '25']
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: E-INT-03
    title: The EHR system follows the EU exchange format recommendation now
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 2
    profiles: [E]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Until EHDS implementing acts apply, the system follows the principles and baseline specifications of
      Commission Recommendation (EU) 2019/243 for patient summaries, ePrescriptions, lab results, images and
      discharge reports.
    rationale: The recommendation is the basis for the European EHR exchange format that the EHDS makes binding.
    improvement: Map your data model to the recommended specifications; plan the gaps.
    effort: high
    sources: [EC-REC-EHRXF, HL7-FHIR]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: M-USE-01
    title: Usability engineering covers use errors
    level: MUST
    tier: 2
    profiles: [M]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The manufacturer applies a usability engineering process: user profiles and use environments, use-related
      risk analysis, formative tests during design and a summative test with representative users before release.
    rationale: MDR Annex I (sections 5 and 22) asks to reduce risks from use errors; IEC 62366-1 is the harmonised standard for doing so.
    improvement: Write the usability engineering file; run a summative test with real users before each major release.
    effort: high
    sources: [MDR, IEC-62366-1]
    detection:
      method: manual

  # ======================================================================= Layer 3: research on design, UX and aesthetics
  - id: CORE-DES-01
    title: Risks and numbers are shown in ways people understand
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Risks and results use natural frequencies ("3 in 100 people") and icon arrays, not only percentages or
      relative risk. The same denominator is used across comparisons.
    rationale: Icon arrays improved understanding of medical risks for people with low and high numeracy, including older adults (Galesic 2009).
    improvement: Replace percentage-only risk displays with frequency statements and an icon array of 100.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-GALESIC2009, R-HLS-EU2015]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-02
    title: Saying no is as easy as saying yes
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      On the first consent screen, "refuse" has the same size, colour weight and position as "accept", and the
      choices for each purpose are on the first screen.
    rationale: Removing the opt-out from the first page raised consent by 22 to 23 points; granular first-page choices lowered it by 8 to 20 points (Nouwens 2020). Real choice needs equal buttons.
    improvement: Redesign the consent screen with equal buttons and per-purpose toggles off by default.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-NOUWENS2020, EDPB-DECEPTIVE]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-03
    title: The visual design is calm, consistent and honest
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The visual design is consistent, readable and calm. Good looks are used to make the product clearer, never to
      make a risk, a cost or a data choice look smaller. Aesthetic changes are tested with users.
    rationale: >
      Perceived beauty shapes perceived usability, even more than actual usability (Tractinsky 2000). This is a
      strength for trust and a risk for over-trust. MARS rates aesthetics as one of four quality dimensions.
    improvement: Keep a design system; check that warnings and costs stay visible in every theme; test redesigns.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-TRACTINSKY2000, R-MARS2015]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-04
    title: Quality is rated before release
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      Before major releases, experts rate the product with MARS and users with uMARS (engagement, functionality,
      aesthetics, information quality), and the team acts on low scores.
    rationale: MARS is a reliable, widely used scale for health app quality (Stoyanov 2015).
    improvement: Add a MARS rating to the release checklist; track scores over versions.
    effort: low
    sources: [R-MARS2015, ISO-82304-2]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-05
    title: Designed and tested with people who find health information hard
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      User research and tests include people with limited health literacy, older adults and people with
      disabilities. Key information has an easy-to-read version.
    rationale: Limited health literacy is common and higher among people with low education, financial deprivation or old age (HLS-EU 2015). Easy-to-read helps people with low literacy or cognitive disabilities (Publications Office).
    improvement: Recruit these groups for every test round; write easy-to-read versions of onboarding, consent and safety texts.
    effort: medium
    sources: [R-HLS-EU2015, OP-PLAIN, WCAG22]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-DES-06
    title: No guilt, shame or fear to drive engagement
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The product does not use guilt, shame, fear or loss streaks about health to keep people using it or to sell.
      Success is measured by health outcomes and user goals, not time in the app.
    rationale: Emotional steering is a deceptive pattern (EDPB 03/2022); exploiting vulnerability is banned for AI (AI Act Art. 5). CSEF applies the same rule to children.
    improvement: Remove guilt messages and loss streaks; replace engagement KPIs with outcome KPIs.
    effort: low
    sources: [EDPB-DECEPTIVE, AIA-GL-PROHIB, CSEF]
    detection:
      method: manual

  - id: CORE-SAF-05
    title: The evidence plan matches the product's function and risk
    level: SHOULD
    tier: 3
    profiles: [core]
    users: [all]
    requirement: >
      The maker classifies its product by function (from system services to treatment) and plans the evidence that
      fits: higher risk functions need stronger evidence of effect.
    rationale: The NICE evidence standards framework sets evidence tiers by function and risk; health systems and buyers in Europe use similar logic.
    improvement: Place the product in the NICE functional classes; write the evidence plan; review it each year.
    effort: medium
    sources: [NICE-ESF, ISO-82304-2]
    detection:
      method: manual
